module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 506

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/506](https://www.erdosproblems.com/506)
- [El67] Elliott, P. D. T. A., *On the number of circles determined by $n$ points*, Acta Math.
  Acad. Sci. Hungar. (1967), 181–188.
- [BaBa94] Bálintová, A. and Bálint, V., *On the number of circles determined by $n$ points in the
  Euclidean plane*, Acta Math. Hungar. (1994), 283–289.
- [PuSm] Purdy and Smith. No reference found.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos506

open EuclideanGeometry

/--
The number of circles determined by a set of points `P` in the plane: the number of distinct
circles (spheres) passing through at least three of the points of `P`. (Three distinct points lie
on a common circle precisely when they are not collinear, so this counts exactly the circumcircles
of the non-collinear triples of `P`.)
-/
noncomputable def numCircles (P : Set ℝ²) : ℕ :=
  Set.ncard { s : Sphere ℝ² | 3 ≤ {p ∈ P | p ∈ s}.ncard }

/--
What is the minimum number of circles determined by any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, not all on a
circle?

There is clearly some non-degeneracy condition intended here - probably either that not all the
points are on a line, or the stronger condition that no three points are on a line.

The answer is known for $n > 393$ (see `erdos_506.variants.large_n`) but the problem appears to
remain open for small $n$ (see `erdos_506.variants.small_n`).
-/
-- Formalisation notes:
-- * Following Elliott, the non-degeneracy condition used here is the weaker of the two: the points
--   are not all on a line and not all on a circle.
-- * The hypothesis `4 ≤ n` is not a restriction of the problem, but excludes the degenerate range
--   where no admissible configuration exists: fewer than three points are collinear, and any three
--   non-collinear points lie on a common circle, so the set below is empty for `n < 4`.
@[category research open, AMS 51 52]
theorem erdos_506 (n : ℕ) (hn : 4 ≤ n) :
    IsLeast { k : ℕ | ∃ P : Finset ℝ²,
        P.card = n ∧ ¬ Collinear ℝ (P : Set ℝ²) ∧ ¬ Cospherical (P : Set ℝ²) ∧
        numCircles (P : Set ℝ²) = k }
      answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
For $n > 393$ the answer is $\binom{n-1}{2} + 1 - \left\lfloor \frac{n-1}{2} \right\rfloor$
(Elliott [El67], with the correction of Purdy and Smith [PuSm], also reported in [BaBa94]): this is
both a lower bound for every such configuration and is attained, e.g. by a circle with $n - 1$
points together with a single point off the circle.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 51 52]
theorem erdos_506.variants.large_n (n : ℕ) (hn : 393 < n) :
    IsLeast { k : ℕ | ∃ P : Finset ℝ²,
        P.card = n ∧ ¬ Collinear ℝ (P : Set ℝ²) ∧ ¬ Cospherical (P : Set ℝ²) ∧
        numCircles (P : Set ℝ²) = k }
      answer((n - 1).choose 2 + 1 - (n - 1) / 2) := by
  sorry

/--
The problem appears to remain open for small $n$: Elliott's answer is established only for
$n > 393$, so the minimum number of circles determined by $n$ points, not all on a line and not all
on a circle, is unknown for $n \le 393$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51 52]
theorem erdos_506.variants.small_n (n : ℕ) (hn : 4 ≤ n) (hn' : n ≤ 393) :
    IsLeast { k : ℕ | ∃ P : Finset ℝ²,
        P.card = n ∧ ¬ Collinear ℝ (P : Set ℝ²) ∧ ¬ Cospherical (P : Set ℝ²) ∧
        numCircles (P : Set ℝ²) = k }
      answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
Segre's observation: the lower bound $\binom{n-1}{2}$ (without the correction of [PuSm]) is
already false for $n = 8$, as witnessed by the projection of a cube onto a plane. Hence the minimum
number of circles determined by $8$ such points is strictly less than $\binom{7}{2} = 21$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 51 52]
theorem erdos_506.variants.segre_n_eq_eight :
    ∃ P : Finset ℝ²,
      P.card = 8 ∧ ¬ Collinear ℝ (P : Set ℝ²) ∧ ¬ Cospherical (P : Set ℝ²) ∧
      numCircles (P : Set ℝ²) < (8 - 1).choose 2 := by
  sorry

end Erdos506

findings.description: The Lean statement is correct. Only the docstring is imprecise. It says the value C(n-1,2)+1-⌊(n-1)/2⌋ "is attained, e.g. by a circle with n − 1 points together with a single point off the circle". If the extra point p is in generic position (no line through p contains two of the circle points), this configuration determines C(n-1,2)+1 circles: the big circle plus one circle per pair of circle points. That exceeds the stated minimum by ⌊(n-1)/2⌋ ≥ 1. The value is attained only when p lies on ⌊(n-1)/2⌋ lines through disjoint pairs of circle points, e.g. p is the centre and the circle points come in antipodal pairs. A reader could take the docstring to mean that any such configuration is extremal.
findings.source_evidence: Purdy & Smith, 'Lines, Circles, Planes and Spheres', arXiv:0907.0724 (DCG 44 (2010) 860–882), section 'Circles Determined by Points in R^2': "The lower bound is actually 1+C(n-1,2)-⌊(n-1)/2⌋ ... as may be seen by taking a circle with n-1 points on it and a point p off the circle. It is easy to arrange the points such that p lies on ⌊(n-1)/2⌋ threepoint lines." erdosproblems.com/506 uses the looser phrase the docstring copies: "This is best possible, as witnessed by a circle with n-1 points and a single point off the circle."
findings.suggested_fix: Reword to: "... and is attained, e.g. by n − 1 points on a circle, placed in antipodal pairs (with one extra point if n − 1 is odd), together with the centre of the circle."

reformulations.difference: The source asks for the minimum for every n. The Lean adds the hypothesis `4 ≤ n` (also in `erdos_506.variants.small_n`).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For n ≤ 3 no admissible configuration exists. Sets of at most 2 points are collinear, and 3 non-collinear points are affinely independent, so they lie on their circumcircle (`AffineIndependent.existsUnique_dist_eq`) and are cospherical. So the set inside `IsLeast` is empty for n < 4 and the question has no minimum there. Restricting to n ≥ 4 loses no content. I proved in the scratch file that the set is `∅` for every n < 4.

reformulations.difference: Circles are counted as Mathlib `EuclideanGeometry.Sphere ℝ²` structures (a centre and an arbitrary real radius) that contain at least 3 points of P. The count uses `Set.ncard`, which returns 0 on infinite sets, and lines are not counted.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A sphere containing ≥ 3 points has positive radius (proved in scratch). Two distinct spheres in the plane share at most 2 points (Mathlib `eq_of_mem_sphere_of_mem_sphere_of_finrank_eq_two`), so each counted sphere is a genuine circle through ≥ 3 points of P and is never counted twice. For finite P the set of counted spheres is finite (proved in scratch), so `ncard` is the true count. Not counting lines matches the source: the Purdy–Smith term −⌊(n−1)/2⌋ exists exactly because collinear triples determine no circle. This is the standard number of circles determined by P.

review.notes:
No misformalization found. Per declaration:

- `erdos_506` (research open): IsLeast of the circle counts over n-point sets that are neither collinear nor concyclic, with the answer slot depending on n. This matches the question. The site says the non-degeneracy condition is ambiguous: "not all on a line" or "no three on a line". The file picks the weaker condition and documents why. That is the condition Elliott used, and the condition under which the site calls the problem "resolved up to a finite check". The two readings give different problems: the extremal Purdy–Smith configuration has collinear triples, so under "no three collinear" the answer for large n would likely be C(n−1,2)+1. I consider the file's choice legitimate. A variant for the other reading could be added, but its absence is not a defect.
- `large_n` (research solved): IsLeast at `(n - 1).choose 2 + 1 - (n - 1) / 2` for n > 393. The truncated ℕ subtraction never bites here. The value is attained for every n ≥ 4 by the centre plus n − 1 circle points in antipodal pairs. The lower bound for n ≥ 394 is Purdy–Smith's correction of Elliott ("Elliott's proof can easily be modified to show the correct result with the same lower bound of 394 for n"). This matches the site.
- `small_n` (research open): matches "appears to remain open for small n". The docstring's "unknown for n ≤ 393" overstates slightly: n = 4 is trivially 3, and forum posts claim m(5..8) = 5, 8, 11, 17. The source's own wording is "small n", and the category is fine because the answer as a function on [4, 393] is unknown.
- `segre_n_eq_eight` (research solved): the existence of 8 admissible points with fewer than 21 circles faithfully states "the lower bound C(n−1,2) is false for n = 8". It is true: the cube construction gives 17–20, and circle-plus-centre gives 19.

Status: the site lists #506 as DECIDABLE (open, reduced to a finite check). The page was last edited 01 Feb 2026. There is one unverified AI-assisted 'full proof' claim (R. Wrona, Aug 2026) that the site has not accepted. The open/solved tags are consistent with this and with the pattern used for Erdős 551.

Reference: the module docstring says "[PuSm] Purdy and Smith. No reference found." The erdosproblems forum identifies it as G. B. Purdy and J. W. Smith, "Lines, Circles, Planes and Spheres", DCG 44 (2010) 860–882, arXiv:0907.0724, which contains the correction verbatim. Maintainers may want to add this citation.

Primary papers I could not read: Elliott 1967 (paywalled) and Erdős 1961 (a scan). I relied on the site's and Purdy–Smith's consistent accounts of Elliott's hypotheses and threshold.
